docs.title: Void
docs.text:
Void is a Wayland compositor without policy. It is a programmable scene, not a desktop.

Void has no window manager, no layout, no keybindings and no look. The core renders a small scene of primitives and offers one API. Plugins add all other behavior. A plugin can supply a stacking desktop, a tiling workflow, or a view that an agent arranges live by voice. Only a small safety layer is built in.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Concept phase. The repository holds the design documents. There is no code yet.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text: The documentation lives in docs/ and on https://marpogaus.github.io/void/.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: See CONTRIBUTING.md.

docs.title: Use of LLM coding tools
docs.text: This project uses LLM coding tools for design, code and documentation.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text: Every part of Void gets a check against existing projects. This page records the first check from October 2026. An entry with the mark unverified needs a second look.

docs.title: Compositors
docs.text:
Project Stack Extension model Fit for Void Missing River 0.4 Zig, wlroots the window manager is a separate process; it speaks the stable river-window-management-v1 protocol with atomic, frame-perfect updates closest to "the window manager is a plugin" no scene graph, no shaders or effects Pinnacle Rust, Smithay gRPC API with Lua and Rust clients; Snowcap widgets best Rust base for a fork: the policy already lives outside the compositor no scene primitives, no shader nodes, no MCP; small team niri Rust, Smithay KDL config, niri msg IPC, no plugins best Smithay reference for rendering, shaders, blur and animations scrolling tiling is built in cosmic-comp Rust, Smithay none production-grade Smithay reference bound to COSMIC Jay Rust, own stack config as a Rust library (unverified) reference for a Vulkan renderer not Smithay; GPLv3 Wayfire C++, wlroots in-process C++ plugins, IPC close plugin idea, 3D effects unsafe C++ ABI, slow releases Hyprland C++, Aquamarine C++ plugins with an unstable ABI, Lua config the target effects opinionated; the plugin ABI breaks with every release Mir and MirAL C++ libraries for shells mature C++; the policy model of MirAL Louvre C++ library with defaults that can be replaced good scene API not Rust scenefx C, wlroots wlroots scene with blur, shadows and rounded corners scene graph and effects C and wlroots only CwC, SomeWM, Strata C and Lua, Rust and Lua scripted configs scriptable no policy-free core with a scene graph

Agent tools exist today only as external MCP servers on top of existing compositors, for example kwin-mcp, and hypruse for Hyprland. The check found no compositor with WASM plugins or built-in MCP. The combination of Void appears to be new: a policy-free core, a scene of primitives with shaders, and one API for plugins, IPC and MCP.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
1. Build on Smithay and copy from others. Sources: the anvil and smallvil examples, niri, cosmic-comp, Pinnacle. This option gives full control of the scene and the plugin model. Recommended (P4).
  2. Fork Pinnacle. A working Smithay compositor with an external API on day one. The fork must remove its policy and add the scene, the shaders and the transactions. R9 proposes a short code review before a decision.
  3. River 0.4 with a Rust window manager. No compositor code, but no shaders, no effects and no scene. This option drops the game-engine half of the idea. It is a fallback for a quick tiling prototype.
  4. An MCP server on an existing compositor, like kwin-mcp. This is the fastest way to try agentic workflows. It gives no canvas and no effects.

River shows a strong design for the window manager interface. Void can copy its semantics without its code.

docs.title: Plugin runtimes
docs.text:
Runtime Strengths Weaknesses Extism on wasmtime more than 13 guest languages, simple, sandboxed bytes in, bytes out: every call serializes and copies wasmtime with the Component Model typed WIT interfaces, handles to scene nodes, fuel and epoch limits, fast new instances fewer mature guest languages; Rust is first-class wasmer works less momentum for the Component Model mlua with LuaJIT or Luau low friction, easy reload, Luau sandbox no memory isolation from the host Rhai pure Rust, easy slow tree-walking interpreter Rune native to Rust not at 1.0 deno_core (V8) JS and TS ecosystem heavy, GC pauses, API churn abi_stable dylibs native speed stale, unsafe unloading, no sandbox IPC clients (separate processes) any language, crash isolation from the OS, no runtime in the core a round trip per event; no code in every frame

For code in every frame, the Component Model is better than Extism. Typed calls only help when the boundary stays typed: JSON over WIT gives back the cost of Extism. R1 proposes to start with IPC clients only and to add wasmtime when a measurement demands it.

docs.title: Renderer
docs.text:
• niri, cosmic-comp and Pinnacle use the GLES renderer of Smithay. Custom GLSL shaders through texture and pixel shader elements work in practice, for example the blur of niri.
  • No Smithay compositor renders through wgpu. The Smithay maintainers consider wgpu too abstract for a compositor. Smithay has no merged Vulkan renderer either.
  • Recommendation: GLES and GLSL (P3).

docs.title: MCP
docs.text: rmcp 3.x supports stdio and Streamable HTTP. voidctl mcp uses stdio. A container gets the socket through a bind mount, so Void needs no network transport for now.

docs.title: Widgets and shells
docs.text: Quickshell is the strongest choice: Qt6 and QML, declarative, with live reload. waybar is mature. eww and AGS/Astal need a check of their activity. A webview on gtk4-layer-shell with WebKitGTK, or a Tauri window as a layer surface, shows HTML from agents. All of these need wlr-layer-shell.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Draft

A first sketch of the one API of Void. Names and shapes will change. The principle stays: plugins, IPC clients and agents use one language of commands and events.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
A command changes the scene. An event reports a change. Commands travel in transactions (see Architecture).

# one transaction
- create: {id: work, kind: group, parent: root}
- create: {id: bg, kind: shader, parent: work, shader: aurora.frag}
- attach: {surface: s42, parent: work}
- configure: {surface: s42, size: [900, 600], states: [activated]}
- update: {id: s42, transform: {translate: [40, 40]}}
- update: {id: work, effects: [{shader: blur.frag, uniforms: {radius: 8}}]}
- focus: {surface: s42}

docs.title: Nodes
docs.text:
This table is the one list of node properties.

Property Nodes Meaning id all stable id; the core assigns ids to surfaces transform all translate, scale, rotate, anchor (R6 asks for a 3D matrix) opacity, visible all clip all rectangle, optionally rounded effects all list of shaders with uniforms input all accept, pass or block meta all free key/value pairs to tag and find nodes size rect, image, shader width and height color, radius, border rect source image file path or buffer shader, uniforms shader GLSL ES file (P3) and its inputs

A surface node gets its size from its client. The configure command asks the client for a new size.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Command Purpose create create a group, rect, image or shader node under a parent attach put a detached surface node under a parent update change node properties animate change properties over a duration with an easing curve move change the parent or the position among the siblings remove remove a node; a removed surface becomes detached configure send size, toplevel states (activated, tiled, maximized, fullscreen) and decoration mode to a client focus set the keyboard focus close ask a client to close a surface

animate lets plugins and agents animate without code in every frame (see R1).

docs.title: Selectors
docs.text: A selector finds nodes without an id: id:work, app_id:firefox, title~:Inbox, meta:role=editor, kind:surface. Selectors work in queries only. R8 asks how a selector behaves when several surfaces match.

docs.title: Events
docs.text: Event Data surface.created, surface.destroyed surface id, app_id, title, role (toplevel, layer, popup) surface.changed title, app_id, min and max size, requests for maximize, fullscreen and activation input.key, input.pointer, input.touch, input.gesture event data for grabs output.added, output.removed, output.changed output, mode, scale plugin.connected, plugin.failed name, error transaction.applied, transaction.rejected id, error, for example a shader compile error

docs.title: IPC methods
docs.text:
JSON-RPC 2.0 on the socket in VOID_SOCKET.

Method Purpose scene.query(selector) read nodes scene.apply(transaction) apply a transaction events.subscribe(filter) stream events input.grab(binding) get the events of a key, a button or a gesture input.inject(events) send synthetic input screen.capture(target) capture an output, a group or a surface output.list list the outputs

The core implements wlr-output-management, so kanshi and wlr-randr configure the outputs. The API has no output configuration of its own.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
Proposal R1 makes a plugin an IPC client with a manifest:

name: tiling
exec: void-tiling
subscribe: [surface.created, surface.destroyed, output.changed]
grabs: [Super+h, Super+l]

A plugin owns the nodes that it creates. The core removes them when the plugin disconnects. R3 proposes that plugins also export methods, for example tiling.set_layout, so that agents ask the window manager instead of fighting it.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: R4 proposes that version 1 trusts every client of the same user, as sway does. Input injection and screen capture still need an explicit grant.

docs.title: MCP tools
docs.text: voidctl mcp offers the IPC methods as MCP tools. It also offers tools for whole tasks, for example "describe the screen", which returns a screenshot and the scene tree. The agent then sees the result of its changes.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Draft

This page shows the architecture after the first review. The proposals (P and R) in Decisions can still change it. The page names them where they apply.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph core["void (Rust, Smithay)"]
        protocols["Wayland protocols"]
        backends["Backends: DRM/KMS and libinput, winit for development"]
        scene["Scene: group, surface, rect, image, shader"]
        render["Renderer: GLES and GLSL shaders"]
        input["Input router"]
        ipc["IPC socket: JSON-RPC"]
        safety["Safety layer"]
    end
    clients["Wayland clients: apps, Quickshell, waybar, webviews"] <--> protocols
    plugins["Plugins: WM, layouts, effects, keybindings"] <--> ipc
    voidctl["voidctl: CLI and MCP bridge"] <--> ipc
    services["Services in containers"] <--> ipc
    agents["Agents: MCP clients"] <--> voidctl
    services -.-> clients

The core has one language: commands and events (see API). Plugins, voidctl, services and agents all use it. Nothing outside the core changes the scene in another way.

The diagram shows plugins as IPC clients, as proposal R1 suggests. Decision D7 adds in-process plugins for work in every frame. R1 defers them.

docs.title: Core
docs.text:
The compositor binary void. Its tasks, and nothing more:

  • Wayland protocol handling and the client lifecycle, through Smithay.
  • Backends: DRM/KMS and libinput on real hardware, through libseat. A winit window for development inside another compositor.
  • The scene, rendered every frame.
  • Input routing (see below).
  • The IPC socket.
  • The safety layer (see below).

The core places popups, subsurfaces and layer surfaces itself, because the protocols define their position. Smithay's PopupManager and LayerMap do this work. Only toplevels wait for a plugin: the core creates a detached surface node and sends surface.created. A plugin decides where the surface appears, or if it appears at all.

docs.title: Scene
docs.text:
The scene is a tree of nodes with stable ids. API lists the node properties. The order of the children sets the stacking order.

The crate void-scene holds the scene model (see Project structure).

docs.title: Renderer
docs.text:
The core uses Smithay's GLES renderer through Smithay's own renderer traits (P3). Custom texture and pixel shaders give blur, rounded corners, shadows, color effects and transitions. niri shows what this approach can do. Shaders are GLSL ES. The core compiles them at runtime and reloads them when they change.

Damage tracking keeps the GPU load low. Each shader declares if it is static or animated, and effects expand the damage area. A fullscreen surface without effects goes to direct scanout.

docs.title: IPC socket
docs.text: JSON-RPC 2.0 on a Unix socket. The core exports its path as VOID_SOCKET. voidctl, plugins and services connect to it. Event subscriptions stream over the same connection.

docs.title: voidctl and the MCP bridge
docs.text: voidctl is the CLI for the coordinator. voidctl mcp serves the API as MCP tools over stdio. MCP stays out of the core (P2), so the MCP side can change without a change to the compositor.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
A transaction is a batch of commands. The core applies it as one unit.

Some commands need a client round trip. A resize sends a configure event, and the client must answer with a new buffer. The core therefore holds the transaction until all affected clients commit, or until a deadline passes. Then the core shows all changes in the same frame. Sway, niri and River work the same way.

docs.title: Frame flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Backend
    participant C as Core
    participant R as Renderer
    B->>C: vblank
    C->>C: apply the transactions that are ready
    C->>R: render the damaged parts of the scene
    R-->>B: page flip

docs.title: Input flow
docs.text:
1. libinput sends an event to the core.
  2. The safety layer checks its fixed bindings first.
  3. The plugins that grabbed the key or the pointer get the event. A plugin consumes the event or lets it pass.
  4. The focused surface gets each event that no plugin consumed. Pointer events go to the topmost node under the cursor that accepts input.

Focus is state in the scene, and plugins set it. The core never sets focus by itself. The core still implements the protocol mechanisms around focus: popup grabs, xdg-activation requests, pointer-constraints and input-method.

docs.title: Safety layer
docs.text:
The safety layer is the only built-in behavior (see Vision). No plugin and no IPC client can change it.

  • Fixed bindings for VT switch, quit and emergency reset. Injected input never triggers them.
  • Emergency reset. The core unloads all plugins, removes all effects and puts all surfaces in a simple grid. This grid is the one layout in the core. It is hardcoded, so a broken config cannot break it.
  • Session lock. The core enforces ext-session-lock. The lock surface is above every plugin node.
  • Watchdog. When frames miss their deadline repeatedly, the core removes the effects first and then the plugins.
  • Plugin failure. A plugin that crashes or hangs loses its nodes. Its surfaces become detached, and the core sends an event. The core keeps running.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
• A binary and a void.desktop session file. A display manager then offers Void next to the existing desktops.
  • A derived secureblue image, built with secureblue-images and image-builder-action, installs Void.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Draft

Proposal R2 in Decisions moves views, flavors and services out of the core. This page shows that model.

Views are YAML files in git, and an agent can read and write them. A strict schema validates each file. It rejects unknown keys and catches the YAML traps, for example no read as false.

The core reads no configuration file. It starts one command, usually the systemd target of a flavor:

void -- systemctl --user start tiling.target

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
~/.config/void/
├── views/      # one file per view
├── flavors/    # bundles of views, plugins and services
├── plugins/    # plugin manifests
└── shaders/    # GLSL ES shaders

The directory is a git repository. It contains no secrets.

docs.title: Views
docs.text:
A view is a part of the scene and the plugins that drive it. voidctl view load <name> starts the plugins of the view and applies its nodes as one transaction. Only voidctl starts plugins.

# ~/.config/void/views/analysis.yaml
name: analysis
plugins:
- name: tiling
  config: {layout: columns, gap: 12}
- name: keybindings
  config:
    bindings:
      Super+Return: {spawn: wezterm}
      Super+q: close
scene:
- id: workspace
  kind: group
  effects: [{shader: vignette.frag, uniforms: {strength: 0.3}}]

The tiling plugin places the surfaces in workspace. The view only names the plugin and its configuration.

docs.title: Flavors
docs.text:
A flavor is a directory with views, plugin manifests and services, plus a systemd user target. The target starts the services and then loads the first view with voidctl. systemd handles start, restart and order, so Void needs no service manager.

flavors/agentic/
├── agentic.target
├── views/       # morning, analysis, writing, coding
├── plugins/     # canvas layout, keybindings
└── services/    # Quadlet units: speech, webview host

docs.title: Services
docs.text: A service runs as a Quadlet unit with Podman, or in distrobox. It connects to the IPC socket, appears as a Wayland client, or both. A container gets the IPC socket through a bind mount.

docs.title: Decisions and open questions
docs.text:
The decision log. Nothing here is final. Every entry can come back for review.

  • Decided: agreed in discussion.
  • Accepted after review: corrections from the first review. They follow from the decided principles or from Wayland facts.
  • Proposed: recommendations from the review. They wait for a decision.

docs.title: Decided
docs.text: # Decision Reason D1 Rust and Smithay for the core Smithay is a library without policy, proven in niri and cosmic-comp. Rust is safe when agents change the system live. D2 Everything is a plugin Maximum flexibility and a small core. D3 An experimentation platform first, then a stable, feature-complete core, then testing A small core gives stability. D4 Fedora and secureblue as host; a derived image offers Void as an additional session The system and the image tooling of the author. D5 Services in containers (Podman, distrobox) Isolation, easy to add and remove. D6 The coordinator is the user first, later an agent with special permissions A gradual path to control by agents. D7 Two access levels: the IPC socket, and in-process plugins for work in every frame Low latency where it matters, robustness everywhere else. R1 challenges the second level. D8 A scene of five primitives; text and widgets come from existing Wayland clients No text stack in the core. D9 YAML for views and flavors, with strict schema validation Readability. The schema catches the YAML traps. R2 makes a flavor a directory with a systemd target. D10 One vocabulary, defined in the Glossary One language for people and agents. D11 Inventory and agent memory form a separate layer, not part of the core The platform stays neutral. D12 Reuse before writing; check alternatives for every decision Little code to maintain.

docs.title: Proposed before the review
docs.text:
# Proposal Reason P2 MCP outside the core Keeps the core small. Now voidctl mcp over stdio. P3 GLES renderer and GLSL shaders Proven in niri. No Smithay compositor uses wgpu. P4 Build on Smithay and copy from niri and Pinnacle Full control of the scene and the plugin model. P8 Xwayland through xwayland-satellite Keeps the core small. P10 English for code and documentation The docs become public documentation.

P1 (plugin runtime), P5 (safety), P6 (transactions), P7 (capabilities) and P9 (Smithay pin) moved into the lists below.

docs.title: Accepted after review
docs.text: # Change Reason A1 A transaction completes when all affected clients commit, or when a deadline passes A resize needs a client round trip. Sway, niri and River do the same. A2 The core places popups, subsurfaces and layer surfaces; only toplevels wait for a plugin The protocols define these positions. Smithay implements them. A3 A configure command for size, toplevel states and decoration mode; events with size limits and activation requests A window manager needs them. A4 Hardcoded safety layer: fixed bindings that ignore injected input, a reset to a grid, session lock above all plugins, a frame watchdog A recovery path must not depend on a file that an agent can break. A5 No undo history in the core A destroyed client cannot come back. The reset and the views in git cover recovery. A6 A plugin owns its nodes; the core removes them when the plugin stops No orphaned nodes. A7 No z property, no query inside transactions, no plugin state store, no shader.compile, no view.diff in the core Each duplicated another mechanism. A8 Smithay's renderer traits, without an extra abstraction layer Smithay already has the interface. A9 Three crates to start: void-scene, void, voidctl A crate comes when a second consumer needs it. A10 Output configuration through wlr-output-management kanshi and wlr-randr exist. A11 The socket path in VOID_SOCKET, no token store in the config The config lives in git. A12 Pin a Smithay git revision No release since 0.7.0. A13 Shaders declare static or animated; fullscreen surfaces without effects use direct scanout Damage tracking and battery life.

docs.title: Proposed after review
docs.text: # Proposal Reason R1 Plugins are IPC clients first, like the window managers of River; the core offers animate; wasmtime only when a measurement demands it Agents work in seconds, not frames. One runtime less. Typed WIT only helps without JSON. R2 Views, flavors and services leave the core: voidctl loads views, a flavor is a systemd target, a service is a Quadlet unit; the core reads no config Policy and service management do not belong in the core. systemd exists. R3 Write ownership: one writer at a time changes a node; plugins export methods, for example tiling.set_layout A6 settles who removes a node. R3 settles who changes it. Otherwise an agent and the window manager fight over the same nodes. R4 Version 1 trusts the same user, as sway does; wp-security-context-v1 hides privileged protocols from sandboxed clients; containers get restricted sockets; input injection and screen capture need approval Simple first, safe for containers. R5 One logical scene; each output is a viewport onto it Coordinates, scale and multiple outputs depend on this. It also gives the infinite canvas. R6 A 3D matrix transform instead of a 2D transform Cube, wobbly windows and 3D surfaces need it. R7 Defer the image node, or support PNG only Image decoding in the core costs code. R8 Define selector behavior for several matches, no match and changed titles Agents depend on predictable results. R9 A short, timeboxed review of the Pinnacle code before P4 is final A fork could save work. R10 First milestone: nested winit core, scene, transactions, IPC, one tiling plugin as IPC client; no WASM, MCP, shaders or flavors The smallest proof of the concept.

docs.title: Rejected review findings
docs.text: Finding Reason Versioned docs with mike are too much The project conventions use mike. Hooks without matching files, and commitizen-branch next to commitizen The project conventions use this hook set in every repository. Cargo hooks before the first crate Requested from the start. They stay inactive until the first Rust file.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
1. Name. "Void" collides with Void Linux. Does that matter for package names and search?
  2. License. MIT or Apache-2.0 like Smithay, or GPL like niri?
  3. Webview host. WebKitGTK, Tauri or Servo? The agentic scenario depends on it.
  4. Hardware. Which GPU vendors come first? NVIDIA?
  5. Screen sharing. A portal backend of its own, or xdg-desktop-portal-wlr?

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: The parts that Void plans to reuse. Each entry is a candidate until Alternatives and Decisions confirm it.

docs.title: Core
docs.text: Dependency Purpose Notes Smithay Wayland protocols, backends, GLES renderer, input a library without policy; used by niri, cosmic-comp and Pinnacle; the latest release is 0.7.0 (June 2025), so Void pins a git revision libinput, libseat, udev, GBM, Mesa hardware access through Smithay calloop event loop Smithay is built on it; the IPC socket shares it serde, schemars API types, generated JSON Schemas a maintained YAML crate views, read by voidctl (R2) serde_yaml is unmaintained rmcp voidctl mcp the official Rust MCP SDK, version 3.x wasmtime in-process plugins (D7); R1 defers them Component Model with typed WIT interfaces

docs.title: Wayland protocols
docs.text:
The core speaks these protocols, so existing tools work unchanged:

  • Base: xdg-shell, xdg-decoration, viewporter, fractional-scale, linux-dmabuf, presentation-time, xdg-output, cursor-shape, data device, primary-selection.
  • Shells and widgets: wlr-layer-shell, ext-foreign-toplevel-list, wlr-foreign-toplevel-management, xdg-activation.
  • Desktop integration: ext-session-lock, ext-idle-notify, idle-inhibit, text-input, input-method, pointer-constraints, relative-pointer, wlr-output-management.
  • Capture: ext-image-copy-capture and wlr-screencopy, and a portal for screen sharing.
  • Isolation: wp-security-context-v1, to hide privileged protocols from sandboxed clients.
  • Xwayland: through xwayland-satellite, a separate process outside the core (P8).

docs.title: Outside the core
docs.text: Tool Role Quickshell, waybar, eww, AGS/Astal bars, panels, widgets fuzzel, wofi launchers a webview host on gtk4-layer-shell and WebKitGTK, or Tauri HTML from agents as surfaces whisper.cpp or faster-whisper, piper speech in and out Podman with Quadlet, distrobox, systemd user units services and flavors kanshi, wlr-randr output configuration

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
The shared vocabulary of Void. Code, docs and prompts to agents use these terms and no synonyms.

Term Meaning Core The compositor process. It handles the Wayland protocols, the backends (DRM/KMS, libinput), the scene, the renderer, the input routing, the IPC socket and the safety layer. It contains no policy. Scene The tree of nodes that the core renders every frame. It is the single source of truth for the screen content. Node One element of the scene. The kinds are group, surface, rect, image and shader. Every node has an id, a transform, an opacity and optional effects. Group A node that contains other nodes. It applies a transform, a clip, an opacity and optional effects to its children. Canvas A group that serves as a working area: a workspace, a desktop or an infinite zoomable plane. Surface A node that shows a Wayland client: an application window, a layer-shell widget or a webview. For the core, a surface is a texture source and an input target. Rect A colored rectangle with optional rounded corners and border. Image A texture from a file or a buffer. Shader A node that a fragment shader draws completely. A shader can also be an effect. Effect A shader that changes how a node and its children look, for example blur or a color change. Every node can have effects. Toplevel A surface with the role of an application window (xdg_toplevel). Other roles are layer surfaces and popups. Detached The state of a surface node without a parent. A detached surface is not visible. View A declarative arrangement: nodes, the plugins that drive them, and their configuration. A view is a YAML file in git. The user or an agent changes it live. Plugin Logic that reacts to events and changes the scene. A window manager, a layout, an animation and a keybinding set are plugins. See Decisions for the plugin runtime. Service A process in a container, outside the core. Examples are speech recognition, a local LLM, a webview host and a development environment. Configuration shows how services run. Flavor A preconfigured bundle of views, plugins and services, for example "classic", "tiling" or "agentic". Coordinator The party that installs and connects plugins, services and flavors. First the user, later an agent with special permissions. Inventory A local, git-versioned store of reusable elements (views, plugins, widgets). It belongs to the opinionated layer above Void, not to the core. Capability A permission of an IPC client or a plugin, for example to read the scene, to inject input or to capture the screen. Command A request to change the scene, for example create or update. Event A message from the core about a change, for example surface.created. Selector An expression that finds nodes without an id, for example app_id:firefox. Safety layer The only built-in behavior of the core: fixed bindings, emergency reset, session lock, watchdog. Transaction A batch of scene commands that the core applies as one unit. If one command fails, the core applies none of them.

docs.title: Idea backlog
docs.text: All ideas that are not decisions yet. An idea moves to Decisions or leaves the list.

docs.title: Interaction
docs.text:
• Voice as the main channel to an agent: speech to text in, text to speech out, with a robust push-to-talk or wake-word mechanism.
  • A morning view: greeting, current tasks, sorted email, and a day plan that user and agent prioritize together.
  • A view for each task, built on demand: data analysis with data, plots and interactive exploration; email; web research; coding.
  • Live changes by voice: resize, rearrange, highlight, dim, switch views.
  • Views that fit the task and the taste of the user. The agent learns the layout preferences of the user.

docs.title: Visuals
docs.text:
• Effects like in Hyprland and Compiz: blur, shadows, rounded corners, wobbly windows, cube, overview, transitions.
  • An infinite zoomable canvas.
  • Surfaces as 3D objects.
  • Pixel-perfect copies of existing desktops (Windows XP, KDE Plasma) as flavors. They prove the flexibility. They are not a goal.

docs.title: Agents and the ecosystem around Void
docs.text:
• An inventory: a local, git-versioned store of reusable elements. Code for one-time use goes away, useful code stays.
  • Agent memory in the home directory.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
• A local inference engine (LLM) in a container.
  • Speech services (whisper, piper).
  • Development environments with special configurations (distrobox).
  • A webview host for HTML that agents generate.

docs.title: Platform
docs.text:
• Flavors as installable bundles: classic, tiling, agentic.
  • A later registry for plugins and flavors, possibly as OCI artifacts. OCI fits the container world of the host.

docs.title: Project structure
docs.text:
The planned layout of this repository: one Cargo workspace with as few crates as possible. A module moves into its own crate only when a second consumer needs it. No crate exists yet.

void/
├── crates/
│   ├── void-scene/   # scene model, commands, events, transactions, selectors; no Smithay
│   ├── void/         # the compositor: Smithay, backends, renderer, input, safety, IPC, plugin host
│   └── voidctl/      # CLI over the IPC socket; `voidctl mcp` is the MCP bridge
├── plugins/          # reference plugins: tiling, stacking, keybindings
├── dist/             # void.desktop session file, packaging
├── docs/             # this documentation (MkDocs)
├── mkdocs.yml
└── Cargo.toml        # workspace, lints

docs.title: Reasons for this split
docs.text:
• void-scene has no Smithay dependency. Tests of the data model and the transaction logic need no GPU and no compositor. The core, voidctl and plugins share this one definition of the API.
  • Reference plugins live in this repository first. They keep the API honest. They can move out when the API is stable.
  • The build generates the schemas from the Rust types. The repository does not contain them. Docs, validation and agents then see the same contract.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text: Three scenarios test the concept and estimate the effort on top of the core. The estimates are rough. They assume that the core implements the common Wayland protocols (see Dependencies), so existing tools work unchanged.

docs.title: 1. Classic desktop
docs.text:
A Windows-like desktop with taskbar, start menu and overlapping windows, driven by mouse and keyboard. This is not the goal of Void, but it must be possible.

Part Source Effort Stacking window manager: move, resize, raise, focus, minimize plugin about 1000 to 2000 lines Window decorations: title bar, buttons plugin with rect and image nodes, or client-side decorations small to medium Keybindings: Alt+Tab, Super key plugin small Taskbar, tray, clock existing shell: Quickshell, waybar, eww configuration Start menu, launcher fuzzel, wofi or a Quickshell widget configuration Pixel-perfect XP look theme assets, shaders, decorations much detail work, little difficulty

The taskbar needs the foreign-toplevel protocols to see the windows. The launcher and the bar need wlr-layer-shell. Dependencies lists all protocols.

Result: medium effort, almost all of it in one window manager plugin.

docs.title: 2. Keyboard-driven tiling
docs.text:
A Linux-style tiling workflow with workspaces. The user configures it.

Part Source Effort Tiling layout: master and stack, columns, scrolling plugin a few hundred lines Workspaces one group per workspace, switched by visibility or transform small Keybindings, focus movement plugin small Bar waybar or Quickshell configuration Animations plugin that animates group transforms small

Result: low effort. This is a good first flavor to test the plugin API.

docs.title: 3. Agentic workday
docs.text:
This scenario is the core idea. A robust voice channel connects the user to an agent, and the agent arranges content for each task.

  1. Morning view. The agent greets the user and shows the current tasks. It sorts the email. User and agent plan and prioritize the day together.
  2. Task views. The agent builds a new canvas for each task and fills it. A data analysis gets prepared data, plots and interactive exploration. Email, web research and coding get their own views.
  3. Reuse. The inventory keeps useful elements in git for later use. The agent discards code for one-time use.
  4. Live change by voice. "Make the plot bigger." "Put the terminal next to the notebook." "Dim everything except the editor."
Part Source Effort Scene access for the agent core IPC and MCP bridge part of the API Speech in and out services: whisper.cpp or faster-whisper, piper integration The agent Claude Code or another MCP client, later a local LLM service integration Rich content: greeting, plots, email the agent writes HTML, a webview host shows it as a surface small service, generated content Data exploration Jupyter, marimo or a plot web app as surfaces existing tools One view per task YAML views, loaded, saved and changed live coordinator feature Inventory, memory opinionated layer above Void later

Result: the largest scenario, but mostly integration of existing parts. The core must supply scene queries and changes, screenshots and input injection. Input injection and screen capture need an explicit grant. The agent needs screenshots to see the result of its changes.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
• The five node kinds cover all three scenarios.
  • Text and widgets do not need to live in the core. Existing shells and a webview host supply them.
  • Two core features decide the success. The protocol coverage lets existing tools work. The API lets plugins and agents arrange everything.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
A desktop decides the arrangement of the content: windows, panels, workspaces. Void takes this decision out of the compositor. Void is a programmable scene. It works more like a game engine than like a window manager. The core renders a scene of nodes every frame. One API changes the scene live.

The motivating use case is agentic interaction. The user talks to an agent, ideally by voice. The agent arranges the screen for the current task and for the taste of the user. Examples are a morning view, a data exploration view and a coding view. The agent changes the arrangement while the user works.

Agents are the motivation, not a requirement. The same scene can host a pixel-perfect Windows XP desktop, a keyboard-driven tiling setup or a KDE-like workflow. It can also host a kind of human-machine interaction that does not exist yet. Void ships none of them. Void makes all of them possible.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
1. Everything is a plugin. The core has no policy: no layout, no focus model, no keybindings, no decorations, no defaults. The window manager is a plugin too. A core without plugins shows a black screen.
  2. Safety is the only built-in behavior. The core keeps an escape hatch that no plugin can override: VT switch, quit, and an emergency reset to a safe state. Agents will write broken code live, so this exception is necessary.
  3. Lean core, fast stability. A small core reaches feature completeness fast. Then the project hardens it. Features grow in plugins, not in the core.
  4. Reuse before writing. Wayland protocol handling, rendering, plugin runtimes, widgets, shells and services already exist. Void connects these parts and writes only what is missing. Fixes go upstream. Every decision gets a check for existing alternatives.
  5. One API for every caller. Plugins, scripts, the CLI, services and agents use the same scene language. An agent can change everything that a user can configure, and it can change it live.
  6. Live and real time. Changes apply while the session runs. They need no restart and cause no noticeable latency.
  7. Declarative and versioned. The configuration is plain text in git: views in YAML, and flavors as bundles of files. A diff shows each change. An agent can read and write the files easily.
  8. Isolation by default. Plugins run as separate processes, services in containers. Sensitive actions, for example input injection and screen capture, need an explicit grant (see Decisions, R4).

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Start as an experimentation platform. Reach a stable, feature-complete core fast, then start testing.
  • Run as an additional session on a Fedora host, next to the existing desktops. The concrete host is a derived secureblue image.
  • Add features as plugins and as services in containers (Podman, distrobox).
  • Let a coordinator install and connect plugins and services. The first coordinator is the user. A later coordinator is an agent with special permissions that can also write new plugins and services.
  • Make it possible to rebuild any existing workflow, with effort, and to invent new ones.

docs.title: Non-goals for now
docs.text:
• A usable desktop out of the box. A flavor can supply one. The core never does.
  • Agent memory and a local inventory of reusable elements. These form a separate, opinionated layer on top of Void (see Idea backlog).
  • Distributions other than Fedora and secureblue, and hardware other than the hardware of the author, until the core is stable.
